sources.title: Presenting the cohomology of a Schubert variety: Proof of the minimality conjecture
sources.summary: Abstract A minimal presentation of the cohomology ring of the flag manifold was given in A. Borel (1953). This presentation was extended by E. Akyildiz–A. Lascoux–P. Pragacz (1992) to a nonminimal one for all Schubert varieties. Work of V. Gasharov–V. Reiner (2002) gave a short, that is, polynomial‐size, presentation for a subclass of Schubert varieties that includes the smooth ones. In V. Reiner–A. Woo–A. Yong (2011), a general shortening was found; it implies an exponential upper bound of on the number of generators required. That work states a minimality conjecture whose significance would be an exponential lower bound of on the number of generators needed in worst case, giving the first obstructions to short presentations. We prove the minimality conjecture. Our proof uses the Hopf algebra structure of the ring of symmetric functions.

sources.summary: A minimal presentation of the cohomology ring of the flag manifold $GL_n/B$ was given in [A. Borel, 1953]. This presentation was extended by [E. Akyildiz-A. Lascoux-P. Pragacz, 1992] to a non-minimal one for all Schubert varieties. Work of [Gasharov-Reiner, 2002] gave a short, i.e. polynomial-size, presentation for a subclass of Schubert varieties that includes the smooth ones. In [V. Reiner-A. Woo-A. Yong, 2011], a general shortening was found; it implies an exponential upper bound of $2^n$ on the number of generators required. That work states a minimality conjecture whose significance would be an exponential lower bound of $\sqrt{2}^{n+2}/\sqrt{πn}$ on the number of generators needed in worst case, giving the first obstructions to short presentations. We prove the minimality conjecture. Our proof uses the Hopf algebra structure of the ring of symmetric functions.

19: 1. Introduction
20: 1.1. Background
21: Let X=Fl_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) be the complete flag manifold ; its points are complete flags of subspaces of {\mathbb{C}}^{n},
22: F_{\bullet}=\{\langle\vec{0}\rangle\subset F_{1}\subset F_{2}\subset\cdots\subset F_{n-1}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\},
23: where F_{i} is a i-dimensional linear subspace of {\mathbb{C}}^{n}.
24: In 1953, A. Borel [ 2 ] gave a presentation of its integral cohomology ring:
25: H^{*}(X)\cong{\mathbb{Z}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]/I^{S_{n}},
26: where I^{S_{n}} is the ideal generated by symmetric polynomials of positive degree. A feature of Borel’s presentation is its shortness : the ideal I^{S_{n}} is generated by the elementary symmetric polynomials
27: e_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), 1\leq i\leq n. This exhibits that H^{*}(X) is a complete intersection, with n generators and n relations.
28: Let GL_{n} be the Lie group of invertible n\times n matrices and B its Borel subgroup of invertible upper triangular matrices. GL_{n} acts transitively on X
29: whereas B is the stabilizer of the standard basis flag given by F_{i}:={\rm Span}\ \{\vec{e}_{1},\vec{e}_{2},\ldots,\vec{e}_{i}\}. By the orbit-stabilizer theorem, X may be
30: identified (topologically) with GL_{n}/B. The finitely many B-orbits of X are called the Schubert cells X_{w}^{\circ} and are indexed by permutations w in the symmetric group S_{n} of permutations of \{1,2,\ldots,n\}. Each cell is isomorphic to the affine space
31: {\mathbb{C}}^{\ell(w)}. Together, they form a CW-decomposition for X where each cell has even real dimension.
32: Their closures, the Schubert varieties
33: X_{w}\coloneqq\overline{X_{w}^{\circ}},
34: provide a {\mathbb{Z}}-basis of the integral homology H_{*}(X) and their
35: Poincaré duals
36: \sigma_{w}=[X_{w}]^{*}
37: give a {\mathbb{Z}}-basis for the integral cohomology ring H^{*}(X).
38: The Bruhat decomposition is
39: X_{w}=\coprod_{u\leq w}X_{u}^{\circ},
40: where u\leq w refers to (strong) Bruhat order on S_{n}. Thus, X_{w} inherits a CW-decomposition from Fl_{n}. The map on cohomology
41: H^{*}(X)\to H^{*}(X_{w})
42: that is induced by the inclusion of X_{w} in Fl_{n} is a surjection with kernel
43: (1)
44: I_{w}\coloneqq\mathrm{Span}_{\mathbb{Z}}\left\{\sigma_{u}\mid u\not\leq w\right\};
45: see [ 12 ] . Therefore one obtains a Borel-type presentation
46: H^{*}(X_{w})\cong H^{*}(X)/I_{w}.
47: The list of generators for I_{w} given in ( 1 ) is quite redundant in general since they span I_{w} linearly . What are more efficient lists of generators for I_{w}?

49: i.e. , a position k such that u(k)>u(k+1).

53: In 2002, V. Gasharov–V. Reiner [ 7 ] showed that when X_{w}

55: given by M. Develin–J. Martin–V. Reiner [ 3 ] .
56: Can one always give such a “short” presentation of
57: H^{*}(X_{w})? Formally, one asks:
58: Is it always possible to generate I_{w} by O({\sf poly}(n)) many generators?
59: In 2011, V. Reiner, A. Woo, and the second author [ 12 ] further refined Theorem 1.1 . Complementing this result was a minimality conjecture which, if true, implies a
60: negative answer to the above question. That is, there is a family of Schubert varieties X_{w^{(n)}} for which I_{w^{(n)}} requires exponentially many generators.

248: A skew diagram is obtained from two partitions \nu and \lambda with
249: \lambda\subseteq\nu by aligning the northwest box of each and taking the set difference. This diagram is
250: denoted \nu/\lambda. Any partition \theta is also a skew diagram \theta=\theta/(0).
251: A picture between two skew diagrams is a bijection between their boxes such that if a box A is weakly above and weakly left of a box B in either diagram, then the corresponding boxes A^{\prime} and B^{\prime} of the other diagram appear in order in the reverse row numbering (the numbering of boxes right-to-left in each row, working top-to-bottom). 20: Abstract.
21: We extend the short presentation due to [Borel ’53] of the cohomology
22: ring of a generalized flag manifold to a relatively short presentation
23: of the cohomology of any of its Schubert varieties. Our result is
24: stated in a root-system uniform manner by introducing the essential set of a Coxeter group element , generalizing and giving a
25: new characterization of [Fulton ’92]’s definition for permutations.
26: Further refinements are obtained in type A.
27: Key words and phrases:
28: Schubert calculus, Schubert variety, cohomology presentation, bigrassmannian, essential set
29: 2000 Mathematics Subject Classification:
30: 14M15, 14N15
31: 1. Introduction
32: The cohomology of the generalized flag manifold G/B, for any complex
33: semisimple algebraic group G and Borel subgroup B, has a classical
34: presentation due to Borel [ B53 ] . Pick a maximal torus
35: T\subset B\subset G, choose a field \Bbbk of characteristic zero, and let
36: V=\Bbbk\otimes_{{\mathbb{Z}}}X(T), where X(T) is the coweight lattice of
37: T. Let \Bbbk[V]:=\mathrm{Sym}(V^{\star}) be the symmetric algebra for
38: V^{\star}; it naturally carries an action of the Weyl group W:=N_{G}(T)/T. Furthermore let \Bbbk[V]^{W} be the ring of W-invariants
39: of \Bbbk[V], and \Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+} the ideal of \Bbbk[V] generated by
40: the W-invariants of positive degree. A classical theorem of Borel
41: [ B53 ] states that
42: (1.1)
43: H^{*}(G/B,\Bbbk)\cong\Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}).
44: A desirable feature of Borel’s presentation is its shortness: since W
45: acts on V^{\star} as a finite reflection group, by Chevalley’s Theorem,
46: the W-invariants \Bbbk[V]^{W} are a polynomial algebra
47: \Bbbk[f_{1},\ldots,f_{n}], where n:=\dim_{\Bbbk}V is the rank of
48: G [ H90 , Section 3.5] . Hence Borel’s presentation shows
49: that H^{\star}(G/B) is a complete intersection as it has n generators and
50: n relations.
51: There is a second way to describe H^{\star}(G/B) arising from
52: a cell decomposition of G/B. One has
53: \begin{array}[]{rll}G&=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB&\text{(Bruhat decomposition)}\\
54: G/B&=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}X_{w}^{\circ}&\text{(Schubert cell decomposition), with}\\
55: X_{w}^{\circ}&:=BwB/B\cong{\mathbb{C}}^{\ell(w)}&\text{ (open Schubert cell)}.\end{array}
56: Here \ell(w) denotes the Coxeter group length of w under the
57: Coxeter system (W,S), where S are the reflections in the simple
58: roots \Pi among the positive roots \Phi^{+}
59: within the natural root system \Phi associated to our Lie pinning.
60: This gives a
61: CW-decomposition for G/B in which all cells have even real
62: dimension. Hence the fundamental homology classes [X_{w}] of their
63: closures X_{w}:=\overline{X_{w}^{\circ}}, the Schubert varieties ,
64: form a {\mathbb{Z}}-basis for the integral homology H_{\star}(G/B), and their
65: (Kronecker) duals \sigma_{w}:=[X_{w}]^{\star} form the dual {\mathbb{Z}}-basis for
66: the integral cohomology H^{\star}(G/B).
67: The above facts lead to an a priori presentation
68: for H^{\star}(X_{w}); see also [ C92 , Cor. 4.4] and
69: [ GR02 , Prop. 2.1] : The Schubert variety X_{w} is the
70: union of the Schubert cells X_{u}^{\circ} for which u\leq w in the
71: (strong) Bruhat order ; hence it inherits a cell decomposition
72: from the flag variety. Consequently, the map on cohomology
73: H^{\star}(G/B)\rightarrow H^{\star}(X_{w})
74: induced by including X_{w}\hookrightarrow G/B is surjective
75: with kernel
76: (1.2)
77: I_{w}:=\Bbbk\text{-span of }\{\sigma_{u}:u\not\leq w\}.
78: This gives rise to presentations
79: (1.3)
80: \displaystyle H^{\star}(X_{w})
81: \displaystyle\cong H^{\star}(G/B)/I_{w}
82: \displaystyle\text{ working over }{\mathbb{Z}}
83: \displaystyle\cong\Bbbk[V]/\left(I_{w}+\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}\right)
84: \displaystyle\text{ working over }\Bbbk.
85: This presentation ( 1.3 ) involves a generating set ( 1.2 )
86: for I_{w} with at most |W| generators. However, this generating set
87: for I_{w} is wasteful in that it not only generates I_{w} as an ideal but
88: actually spans it \Bbbk- linearly within H^{\star}(G/B).
89: Therefore, a basic question is to request more efficient generating
90: sets for I_{w}. For type A_{n-1}, earlier work
91: [ GR02 ] reduced the |W|=n! upper bound on the number
92: of generators for I_{w} to a polynomial bound of n^{2} for the class
93: of Schubert varieties X_{w} defined by inclusions ; this class
94: includes all smooth X_{w}. Moreover, for a certain subclass of smooth
95: Schubert varieties X_{w} considered originally by Ding
96: [ D97 , D01 ] , they gave a smaller generating set for these I_{w}
97: having only n generators. This latter result was applied in
98: [ DMR07 ] to classify these varieties up to
99: isomorphism and homeomorphism (the generating set ( 1.2 )
100: having proved too unwieldy). One motivation for this work arises from
101: the desire to extend this classification to general Schubert varieties of
102: type A. Experience suggests that presentations for I_{w} that are
103: as simple as possible are best for this purpose.
104: The question of finding
105: simple presentations of I_{w} for other root systems appears to
106: have been less studied.
107: The main goal of this paper is to give a concise and root-system
108: uniform extension of Borel’s presentation that produces for arbitrary
109: w\in W an abbreviated list of generators for I_{w}. Our first main
110: result, Theorem 1.1 , achieves this via a strong
111: restriction on the descent set
112: \mathrm{Des}(u):=\{s\in S:\ell(us) \bullet
113: An element u\in W is grassmannian if |\mathrm{Des}(u)|\leq 1.
114: \bullet
115: An element v\in W is bigrassmannian if both v and v^{-1} are grassmannian.
116: \bullet
117: Given w\in W, the essential set for w, denoted
118: {\mathcal{E}}(w), is the set of u\in W which are minimal in the Bruhat order among those
119: not below w.
120: The nomenclature “essential set” for {\mathcal{E}}(w) is justified in
121: Proposition 4.6 , where we give a new
122: characterization of Fulton’s essential set [ F92 ] for the case
123: of the symmetric group W=S_{n}. Indeed, {\mathcal{E}}(w) has been
124: previously studied from a different point of view: a result of Lascoux
125: and Schützenberger [ LS96 , Théorème 3.6] ,
126: implicit in
127: our first main result below, is that the elements in
128: {\mathcal{E}}(w) are bigrassmannian for any w in W. 1 1 1 For Lascoux
129: and Schützenberger this arises in their work (see also Geck and Kim
130: [ GK97 ] and Reading [ R02 ] ) seeking efficient encodings of the strong Bruhat order; it is perhaps not surprising that
131: it should arise in our search for efficient cohomology presentations
132: as well.
133: Theorem 1.1 .
134: For any w\in W, working in a field \Bbbk of characteristic zero,
135: the ideal I_{w} defining H^{\star}(X_{w}) as a quotient of H^{\star}(G/B) is
136: generated by the cohomology classes \sigma_{u} where u\not\leq w
137: and u is grassmannian.
138: More precisely, I_{w} is generated by the classes \sigma_{u} indexed
139: by those grassmannian u for which there exist some bigrassmannian
140: v in {\mathcal{E}}(w) satisfying both u\geq v and \mathrm{Des}(u)=\mathrm{Des}(v).
141: In type A, a similar result was obtained by Akyildiz, Lascoux, and
142: Pragacz [ ALP92 , Theorem 2.2] . Specifically, they prove the first
143: sentence of Theorem 1.1 , though they do not address the
144: strengthening given by the second sentence. Their methods are mainly
145: geometric, as opposed to our essentially combinatorial arguments. Their
146: work provides, to our knowledge, the first inroads towards an abbreviated
147: generating set for I_{w}.
148: Theorem 1.1 replaces the general upper bound
149: of |W| on the number of generators needed for I_{w} with the bound
150: (1.4)
151: \sum_{s\in S}[W:W_{S\setminus\{s\}}],
152: where, for any subset J\subset S, W_{J} denotes the parabolic
153: subgroup of W generated by J. Our theorem is deduced in
154: Section 2 from a more general result
155: (Theorem 2.4 ) that applies to Hiller’s
156: extension [ H82 , Chapter IV] of Schubert calculus as introduced
157: by Bernstein, Gelfand, and Gelfand [ BGG73 ] and
158: Demazure [ D73 ] to the coinvariant algebras of finite
159: reflection groups W.
160: Section 2 explains and proves Theorem 1.1 .
161: In Section 3 , we exploit the particular form of our
162: generators to derive a straightforward extension to Schubert varieties
163: in any partial flag manifold G/P associated to
164: a parabolic subgroup P of G.
165: Section 4 examines
166: more closely Theorem 1.1 in
167: type A_{n-1}. Here one can take G=GL_{n}({\mathbb{C}}),
168: with B the subgroup of invertible upper triangular matrices,
169: T the invertible
170: diagonal matrices, and W=S_{n} the permutation matrices. The bound
171: on generators
172: for I_{w} in ( 1.4 ) becomes 2^{n},
173: at least a practical improvement on |W|=n!.
174: More importantly,
175: one can be even more explicit and efficient in the
176: generating sets for I_{w}.
177: Identify points of
178: G/B with complete flags
179: \langle 0\rangle\subset V_{1}\subset\cdots\subset V_{n-1}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{n}.
180: Under this identification, each Schubert variety X_{w} is the set of
181: flags satisfying certain specific conditions derived from w of the
182: form \dim_{\mathbb{C}}(V_{r}\cap{\mathbb{C}}^{s})\geq t. The bigrassmannians v
183: comprising {\mathcal{E}}(w) correspond to Fulton’s essential Schubert
184: conditions , a minimal list of such conditions defining the Schubert
185: variety X_{w}. Our second main result (Theorem 4.8 )
186: provides for each bigrassmannian v in W=S_{n} a generating set for the ideal
187: (1.5)
188: J_{v}:=\Bbbk\text{-span of }\{\sigma_{u}:u\geq v\}
189: in type A that is smaller than the one used as a general
190: step (Theorem 2.3 ) in the proof of Theorem 1.1
191: for arbitrary finite Coxeter groups W. Our proof of
192: Theorem 4.8 is based on symmetric function identities that we devise for this
193: purpose.
194: Therefore, concatenating these generating sets for J_{v} gives a generating set for
195: (1.6)
196: I_{w}=\sum_{v\in{\mathcal{E}}(w)}J_{v}
197: that is smaller than the one provided by Theorem 1.1 .
198: We remark that this result subsumes (and slightly improves upon;
199: see Example 4.9 )
200: the generating set of size n^{2} given by [ GR02 ]
201: in the case of Schubert varieties defined by inclusions.
202: Actually, we conjecture that this smaller generating set for J_{v} in
203: type A is minimal (although the generating set ( 1.6 )
204: for I_{w} obtained by concatenation is not always minimal; see
205: Example 4.12 .) The significance of this
206: minimality conjecture, as explained in Section 4.5 , is that
207: it implies an exponential lower bound of at least
208: \binom{n/2}{n/4}\sim\frac{{\sqrt{2}}^{n+2}}{\sqrt{\pi n}}
209: on the number of generators needed for I_{w}, accompanying our
210: exponential upper bound of 2^{n}. Thus one would not be able to expect
211: short presentations for H^{*}(X_{w}) in general, at least in type A.
212: 2. Proof of Theorem 1.1
213: As in Section 1, let \Bbbk be a field of characteristic zero.
214: For v,w in W, define two \Bbbk-linear subspaces J_{v},I_{w} of the cohomology
215: H^{\star}(G/B) with \Bbbk coefficients:
216: (2.1)
217: \displaystyle J_{v}
218: \displaystyle:=\Bbbk\text{-span of }\{\sigma_{u}:u\geq v\}
219: \displaystyle I_{w}
220: \displaystyle:=\Bbbk\text{-span of }\{\sigma_{u}:u\not\leq w\}\left(=\sum_{v\in{\mathcal{E}}(w)}J_{v}\right).
221: Recall the essential set {\mathcal{E}}(w) is the
222: set of all Bruhat-minimal elements of \{v\in W:v\not\leq w\}.
223: The Schubert cell decomposition of G/B shows that both of these
224: \Bbbk-subspaces
225: are actually ideals in the cohomology ring H^{\star}(G/B): one has that
226: I_{w} (respectively J_{v}) is
227: the kernel of the surjection H^{\star}(G/B)\rightarrow H^{\star}(X)
228: induced by the inclusion of the
229: B-stable subvariety X\subseteq G/B, where X=X_{w} (respectively
230: X=\bigcup_{u\not\geq v}X_{u}).

232: bigrassmannians in the Bruhat order on Coxeter groups, originally due
233: to Lascoux and Schützenberger [ LS96 , Théorème
234: 3.6] and Geck and Kim [ GK97 , Lemma 2.3 and
235: Theorem 2.5] .
236: Lemma 2.1 .
237: For any Coxeter system (W,S) and w in W, every element of
238: {\mathcal{E}}(w) is bigrassmannian.

243: bigrassmannian v automatically gives generators for the ideals I_{w}.

247: coinvariant algebras. This emphasizes that the arguments of this

438: 3. Reducing presentations in H^{\star}(G/P) to those in H^{\star}(G/B)
439: We explain in this section how Theorem 2.4
440: leads to a shorter presentation more generally for the cohomology of Schubert
441: varieties in any partial flag manifold.
442: Given J\subset S, one has the parabolic subgroup W_{J} of W
443: generated by J. One also has a corresponding parabolic subgroup P_{J} of G,
444: generated by the Borel subgroup B together with representatives within G
445: that lift the elements J\subset W=N_{G}(T)/T.
446: The Borel picture identifies the cohomology ring
447: of the (generalized) partial flag manifold G/P_{J} as the subring of
448: W_{J}-invariants inside the cohomology of G/B. In other words,
449: the quotient map
450: G/B\overset{\pi}{\rightarrow}G/P_{J}
451: induces the inclusion
452: (3.1)
453: H^{\star}(G/P_{J})\cong H^{\star}(G/B)^{W_{J}}\overset{i}{\hookrightarrow}H^{\star}(G/B).
454: Recall that W^{J} denotes the set of minimum-length coset
455: representatives for W/W_{J}. Inside H^{\star}(G/B), the cohomology
456: classes \{\sigma_{w}:w\in W^{J}\} lie in this W_{J}-invariant
457: subalgebra H^{\star}(G/B)^{W_{J}} and form a \Bbbk-basis identified
458: with the \Bbbk-basis of Schubert cohomology classes \sigma_{wW_{J}}
459: for H^{\star}(G/P_{J}). One also has that the pre-image of Schubert
460: varieties in G/P_{J} are certain Schubert varieties of G/B:
461: specifically,
462: \pi^{-1}(X_{wW_{J}})=X_{w_{\max}},
463: where w_{\max} is the unique maximum -length coset representative in wW_{J}.
464: Working more generally with the Hiller Schubert calculus for any finite Coxeter
465: system (W,S), the inclusion ( 3.1 ) generalizes to the inclusion
466: (3.2)
467: \Bbbk[V]^{W_{J}}/\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}\Bbbk[V]^{W_{J}}\cong\left(\Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+})\right)^{W_{J}}\overset{i}{\hookrightarrow}\Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}).
468: The first isomorphism shown in ( 3.2 )
469: is a consequence of the fact that one has an averaging map
470: (3.3)
471: \begin{array}[]{rll}\Bbbk[V]&\overset{\rho}{\longrightarrow}&\Bbbk[V]^{W_{J}}\\
472: f&\longmapsto&\frac{1}{|W_{J}|}\sum_{w\in W_{J}}w(f)\end{array}

474: \Bbbk[V]^{W}-linear) retraction map for i, meaning that \rho\circ i=1_{\Bbbk[V]^{W_{J}}}. Inside \Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}), the Hiller
475: Schubert polynomials \{S_{w}:w\in W^{J}\} lie in this

477: The retraction in ( 3.3 )
478: also provides the relation between the cohomology presentations

564: 4. Refinements in Type A
565: We investigate further the situation when W is a Weyl group of
566: type A_{n-1}, which exhibits extra features; one can:
567: \bullet
568: be more explicit about bigrassmannians and their essential sets {\mathcal{E}}(w),
569: \bullet
570: produce even smaller generating sets for the ideals
571: I_{w} and J_{v}, which are conjecturally minimal in the case of J_{v}, and
572: \bullet

574: over a field \Bbbk of characteristic zero.
575: 4.1. Schubert conditions and bigrassmannians
576: In type A_{n-1}, points in the variety G/B
577: are identified with complete flags of subspaces
578: \langle 0\rangle\subset V_{1}\subset\cdots\subset V_{n-1}\subset{\mathbb{C}}^{n}
579: having \dim_{\mathbb{C}}V_{i}=i. Pick as our particular base flag \{{\mathbb{C}}^{i}\}_{i=0}^{n}, where {\mathbb{C}}^{i} is spanned by the first i standard
580: basis elements; this flag is fixed by the Borel subgroup B
581: consisting of the invertible upper-triangular matrices within
582: G:=GL_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). Picking the maximal torus T of invertible diagonal
583: matrices, one identifies the Weyl group W=N_{G}(T)/T with the
584: symmetric group S_{n}. The Coxeter generators S for W=S_{n}
585: associated to our Borel subgroup B is the set of adjacent
586: transpositions S=\{(1\leftrightarrow 2),(2\leftrightarrow 3),\ldots,(n-1\leftrightarrow n)\}.
587: The Schubert variety X_{w} corresponding to a
588: permutation w=w_{1}w_{2}\cdots w_{n}\in S_{n} (written in one-line notation)
589: can be defined as the subvariety
590: of flags satisfying the conjunction of the Schubert conditions
591: (4.1)
592: \dim_{\mathbb{C}}(V_{r}\cap{\mathbb{C}}^{s})\geq t
593: where
594: (4.2)
595: t={t}_{r,s}(w):=|\{w_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{r}\}\cap\{1,2,\ldots,s\}|
596: for all r,s=1,2,\ldots,n-1 is the rank function associated to w.
597: Denote the condition ( 4.1 )
598: by C_{r,s,t} (for arbitrary t, not necessarily of the form ( 4.2 )).
599: Note that C_{r,s,t} is vacuous unless t>r+s-n.
600: The following
601: explicit identification of bigrassmannian permutations
602: is well-known and straightforward.
603: Lemma 4.1 .
604: The bigrassmannian permutations (other than the identity) are
605: parameterized by r,s,t with 1\leq t\leq r,s\leq n and t>r+s-n.
606: Let v_{r,s,t,n} denote the unique bigrassmannian permutation
607: v_{1}\ldots v_{n}\in S_{n} such that
608: \bullet
609: \mathrm{Des}(v)=\{(r\leftrightarrow r+1)\}
610: \bullet
611: \mathrm{Des}(v^{-1})=\{(s\leftrightarrow s+1)\} , and
612: \bullet
613: v_{t}=s+1 .
614: Then explicitly we have:
615: (4.3)
616: \displaystyle v_{r,s,t,n}
617: \displaystyle:=(1,2,\ldots,t-1,
618: \displaystyle\qquad s+1,s+2,\ldots,s+r-t+1,
619: \displaystyle\quad\qquad t,t+1,t+2,\ldots,s,
620: \displaystyle\qquad\qquad s+r-t+2,s+r-t+3,\ldots,n).
621: There is a simple relation between these Schubert conditions C_{r,s,t}
622: and the bigrassmannian permutations in W=S_{n}:
623: Proposition 4.2 .
624: Let w\in S_{n}.
625: Then the Schubert condition C_{r,s,t} is satisfied by all flags in X_{w}
626: if and only if v_{r,s,t,n}\not\leq w.
627: Proof.
628: Note C_{r,s,t} is a Schubert condition on X_{w} if and only
629: if t_{r,s}(w)\geq t. It is then straightforward to check that the latter is
630: equivalent to v_{r,s,t,n}\not\leq w using the tableau criterion
631: [ BB05 , Theorem 2.6.3] for comparing elements in the Bruhat ordering.
632: ∎
633: Note that imposing an arbitrary conjunction of Schubert conditions on
634: complete flags cuts out a B-stable subvariety of G/B,
635: but this subvariety may be a reducible
636: union of Schubert varieties rather than a single Schubert variety X_{w}.
637: However, in type A, when one imposes a single Schubert condition, the result is
638: always a (single) Schubert variety. This fact can be
639: traced to special properties of the Bruhat order in type A,
640: first identified by Lascoux and Schützenberger [ LS96 ] ,
641: and exploited further by Geck and Kim [ GK97 ] and Reading [ R02 ] .
642: To explain this, we first recall some terminology.
643: Definition 4.3 .
644: In a poset P, say that an element v is a dissector of P if
645: there exists a (necessarily unique) element w in P for which P
646: decomposes as the disjoint union of the principal order filter above v and the
647: principal order ideal below w:
648: P=\{u\in P:u\geq v\}\quad\bigsqcup\quad\{u\in P:u\leq w\}.
649: Say that an element a in a poset P (which need not be a lattice) is
650: join-irreducible
651: if there does not exist a subset X\subset P with a\not\in X
652: such that a is the least element among all upper bounds for X in P.
653: There are two subtle issues to point out in this definition of
654: join-irreducibles. Firstly, when the finite poset is a lattice , an element
655: is join-irreducible if and only if it covers a unique element.
656: However, for non-lattices, one can have join-irreducibles
657: that cover more than one element.
658: For example, the strong Bruhat order in type A_{2} has four non-minimal, non-maximal elements,
659: each of which is join-irreducible, but two of them cover two elements.
660: Secondly, all of the posets that we will consider have a unique least element,
661: (e.g. in Bruhat order on W, the least element is the identity of W), and this least element
662: is not considered join-irreducible because it is the least element among all upper
663: bounds for the empty set X=\varnothing.
664: Theorem 4.4 .
665: [ LS96 , GK97 , R02 ]
666: (i)
667: In any finite poset, every dissector is join-irreducible. When the
668: poset is the Bruhat order for a Coxeter system (W,S) of type A,B,H_{3},H_{4} or
669: I_{2}(m) , the converse holds: the join-irreducible elements are exactly the dissectors.
670: (ii)
671: In the Bruhat order for any finite Coxeter system (W,S) , every join-irreducible element is bigrassmannian.
672: In type A , the converse holds: the (non-identity) bigrassmannian elements are exactly the join-irreducibles.
673: In particular, in type A, for every bigrassmannian v in W, there exists a (necessarily unique) element
674: w in W for which {\mathcal{E}}(w)=\{v\}.
675: Corollary 4.5 .
676: In type A_{n-1}, a single Schubert condition C_{r,s,t} on the flags
677: in G/B cuts out the Schubert variety X_{w_{r,s,t,n}} in G/B, where
678: w_{r,s,t,n} is the unique element with {\mathcal{E}}(w_{r,s,t,n})=\{v_{r,s,t,n}\}
679: as in Theorem 4.4 .
680: Thus in type A_{n-1}, for any bigrassmannian
681: v_{r,s,t,n}, one has equality of
682: the two ideals J_{v_{r,s,t,n}}=I_{w_{r,s,t,n}} within the coinvariant algebra
683: \Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^{W}_{+}).
684: We remark that, as with v_{r,s,t,n}, one knows w_{r,s,t,n} explicitly
685: (see [ R02 , §8] ):
686: \displaystyle w_{r,s,t,n}
687: \displaystyle=(n,n-1,\ldots,(n-r+t+1),
688: \displaystyle\qquad s,s-1,\ldots,s-t+1,
689: \displaystyle\quad\qquad n-r+t,n-r+t-3,\ldots,s+1,
690: \displaystyle\qquad\qquad s-t,s-t-1,\ldots,1).

692: Next, we explain the relation between what we have called the essential set {\mathcal{E}}(w)
693: for w and Fulton’s essential set of Schubert conditions for X_{w}.
694: Note that there are implications among the various Schubert conditions C_{r,s,t}.
695: Fulton introduced the essential set of a permutation, a set of coordinates
696: \{(r_{i},s_{i})\}\subset n\times n which give an inclusion-minimal subset of
697: Schubert conditions C_{r_{i},s_{i},t} with t=t_{r_{i},s_{i}}(w) that suffice to define
698: X_{w} as a subset of the flag manifold. (See further remarks in Example 4.7
699: below.) Correspondingly, we call these Schubert conditions the
700: essential Schubert conditions for
701: X_{w}; see [ F92 , §3] , [ FP98 , pp. 20-21] , and
702: [ EL96 , §2] .
703: Proposition 4.6 .
704: The Schubert condition C_{r,s,t} implies the Schubert condition C_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}
705: if and only if v_{r,s,t,n}\leq v_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n} in Bruhat order.
706: Therefore in type A_{n-1}, Fulton’s essential set of Schubert conditions C_{r,s,t} for X_{w}
707: correspond bijectively to the elements of the essential set {\mathcal{E}}(w) for w defined for a general
708: Coxeter group.

711: Theorem 4.4 give the following:
712: \displaystyle C_{r,s,t}\text{ implies }C_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime}}\Leftrightarrow

715: \displaystyle\qquad\{u\in W:u\leq w_{r,s,t,n}\}\subseteq\{u\in W:u\leq w_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n}\}

717: \displaystyle\qquad\{u\in W:u\geq v_{r,s,t,n}\}\supseteq\{u\in W:u\geq v_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n}\}
718: \displaystyle\Leftrightarrow
719: \displaystyle\qquad v_{r,s,t,n}\leq v_{r^{\prime},s^{\prime},t^{\prime},n}.

125: The cohomology of the generalized flag manifold $G/B$, for any complex

129: $V=\Bbbk\otimes_{\ZZ} X(T)$, where $X(T)$ is the coweight lattice of
130: $T$.  Let $\Bbbk[V]:=\Sym(V^{\star})$ be the symmetric algebra for
131: $V^{\star}$; it naturally carries an action of the Weyl group $W :=
132: N_G(T)/T$.  Furthermore let $\Bbbk[V]^W$ be the ring of $W$-invariants
133: of $\Bbbk[V]$, and $\Bbbk[V]^W_+$ the ideal of $\Bbbk[V]$ generated by
134: the $W$-invariants of positive degree.  A classical theorem of Borel
135: \cite{Borel} states that
136: \begin{equation}
137: \label{Borel-presentation}
138: H^*(G/B,\Bbbk) \cong \Bbbk[V]/(\Bbbk[V]^W_+).
139: \end{equation}

152: $n$ relations.
